items.title: Python with Chai
items.text: Python with Chai. Learn Python basics while making chai. From variables to while loops, each lesson has a 30-second video and notes. 20 of 20 lessons available (20 lessons · complete). Python basics: Chai is a Python program, Run a function, if-else: how much sugar?, Lists: all the flavours in one place, for loops: try every flavour, Dictionaries: the chai menu card, Mini project: the chai bill, input: ask the customer, try-except: explain, don't crash, while True: keep the shop open, Files: save the bill, Files: read the bill back, Modules: the lucky chai, f-strings: a neat bill, range(): 10 cups at once, Default values: less sugar, Sets: how many customers?, datetime: shop timing, Classes: the chai shop, Finale: you know Python!.

items.title: Python with Chai · Chai is a Python program
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 1: Chai is a Python program.
A chai recipe and a Python program work the same way.
The ingredients (water, milk, tea leaves, sugar) are variables : a name with a value stored in it.
The recipe is a function : write the steps once, run them whenever you want.
"Keep heating until it boils" is a while loop : the work repeats as long as the condition is true.
Remember: If you can make chai, you can learn Python.
Try it yourself: Create 4 variables for the ingredients of your favourite chai. Change temp + 20 to temp + 40 . How many times does the loop run now?
Code:
paani = "1 cup"
cheeni = 1

temp = 20
while temp < 100:
    temp = temp + 20      # keep heating
print("Chai ready!")
Output:
Chai ready!

items.title: Python with Chai · Run a function
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 2: Run a function.
You write a function with def . Writing it doesn't run it; Python just remembers it.
Add () after the name to RUN it. This is called calling the function.
return sends an answer back from the function, which you can store in a variable.
Remember: Functions: write once, run any time.
Try it yourself: Call chai_banao() twice. How many times does the output appear? Write a new function called coffee_banao() .
Code:
def chai_banao():
    print("Paani ubla")
    print("Patti daali")
    print("Doodh daala")
    return "Chai ready!"

cup = chai_banao()
print(cup)
Output:
Paani ubla
Patti daali
Doodh daala
Chai ready!

items.title: Python with Chai · if-else: how much sugar?
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 3: if-else: how much sugar?.
if checks a condition. If it's true, the code inside it runs.
If the condition is false, the else path runs instead.
Two paths, one decision. This is how a computer makes choices.
Remember: if-else is how the computer decides.
Try it yourself: Set cheeni = 0 and run it. What prints now? Add elif cheeni == 1: and print "Normal chai".
Code:
cheeni = 2

if cheeni > 1:
    print("Meethi chai")
else:
    print("Feeki chai")
Output:
Meethi chai

items.title: Python with Chai · Lists: all the flavours in one place
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 4: Lists: all the flavours in one place.
A list is a box that holds many items together, written inside [ ] .
Counting starts at 0, so the first item is flavours[0] .
append() adds a new item, and len() tells you how many items there are.
Remember: A list keeps all the flavours in one place.
Try it yourself: Print flavours[1] . Print flavours[3] before the append. What error do you get, and why?
Code:
flavours = ["Masala", "Adrak", "Elaichi"]

print(flavours[0])
print(flavours[2])
flavours.append("Tulsi")
print(len(flavours))
Output:
Masala
Elaichi
4

items.title: Python with Chai · for loops: try every flavour
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 5: for loops: try every flavour.
With for f in flavours: , each item in the list goes into f , one at a time.
The code inside the loop runs once for each item.
Whether there are 4 items or 100, the code stays just as short.
Remember: A for loop handles every item, one by one.
Try it yourself: Add "Kesar" to the list and run the loop again. Put a number in front of each line (hint: use a count variable).
Code:
flavours = ["Masala", "Adrak", "Elaichi", "Tulsi"]

for f in flavours:
    print(f + " chai")
Output:
Masala chai
Adrak chai
Elaichi chai
Tulsi chai

items.title: Python with Chai · Dictionaries: the chai menu card
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 6: Dictionaries: the chai menu card.
A dictionary stores pairs of keys and values: an item's name and its price.
Give it a key, get the value back: menu["Masala"] gives 20.
Adding an item and changing a price both use menu[key] = value .
Remember: A dictionary lets you look things up by name.
Try it yourself: Build a menu for your own shop with 5 items. Use for naam in menu: to print each item and its price.
Code:
menu = {"Masala": 20, "Adrak": 15, "Elaichi": 25}

print(menu["Masala"])
menu["Tulsi"] = 30     # new item
menu["Adrak"] = 18     # price changed
print(menu)
Output:
20
{'Masala': 20, 'Adrak': 18, 'Elaichi': 25, 'Tulsi': 30}

items.title: Python with Chai · Mini project: the chai bill
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 7: Mini project: the chai bill.
Everything so far, together: the menu is a dictionary and the order is a list.
The bill() function uses a for loop to add up the price of each item.
An if gives a 5 rupee discount on bills over 50.
Remember: You're a Python coder now!
Try it yourself: Add one more "Adrak" to the order. What is the new total? Change the discount to 10%.
Code:
menu = {"Masala": 20, "Adrak": 15}
order = ["Masala", "Adrak", "Masala"]

def bill(order):
    total = 0
    for item in order:
        total += menu[item]
    if total > 50:
        total -= 5
    return total

print("Total:", bill(order))
Output:
Total: 50

items.title: Python with Chai · input: ask the customer
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 8: input: ask the customer.
input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type an answer.
input always gives you text . If you need a number, wrap it in int() .
Without int, "3" * 20 writes "3" twenty times instead of giving 60.
Remember: input lets your program talk to people.
Try it yourself: Also ask for the flavour and take its price from the menu. Remove int() , run it, and look at the output.
Code:
naam = input("Naam? ")
print("Namaste", naam)

cups = int(input("Kitne cup? "))
print("Bill:", cups * 20)
Output:
Naam? Raj
Namaste Raj
Kitne cup? 3
Bill: 60

items.title: Python with Chai · try-except: explain, don't crash
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 9: try-except: explain, don't crash.
If the customer types "teen" instead of a number, int() raises a ValueError and the program crashes.
Put the risky code inside try . If an error happens, except catches it.
The program keeps running and politely tells the user what went wrong.
Remember: try-except: explain the problem instead of crashing.
Try it yourself: Put this code inside a while True loop so it keeps asking until it gets a valid number (see Lesson 10).
Code:
try:
    cups = int(input("Kitne cup? "))
    print("Bill:", cups * 20)
except ValueError:
    print("Number likho!")
Output:
Kitne cup? teen
Number likho!

items.title: Python with Chai · while True: keep the shop open
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 10: while True: keep the shop open.
while True means keep going forever: take an order, serve chai, next order.
break exits the loop immediately.
To close the shop, type "band". The if and break stop the loop.
Remember: while True keeps going; break stops.
Try it yourself: Add every order to a list and print all the orders when the shop closes. Add the try-except from Lesson 9 and also ask how many cups.
Code:
while True:
    order = input("Order? ")
    if order == "band":
        break
    print(order, "ready!")
print("Dukaan band! Kal milte hain.")
Output:
Order? Masala
Masala ready!
Order? band
Dukaan band! Kal milte hain.

items.title: Python with Chai · Files: save the bill
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 11: Files: save the bill.
A variable lives only in memory (RAM). When the program closes, its value is gone.
A file stays on the disk, like the shop's register book: it is still there tomorrow.
open("bill.txt", "w") opens a file for writing , and with closes it for you automatically.
Remember: A variable forgets; a file remembers.
Try it yourself: Run it, then open bill.txt in Notepad. What's inside? Write 3 lines into the file (hint: add \n at the end of each line).
Code:
total = 50

with open("bill.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Total: Rs " + str(total))

print("Bill saved!")
Output:
Bill saved!
(bill.txt now contains: Total: Rs 50)

items.title: Python with Chai · Files: read the bill back
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 12: Files: read the bill back.
open("bill.txt", "r") opens a file for reading , and read() gives you all its text.
"w" wipes the file and writes it fresh; "a" (append) keeps what is there and adds to the end.
So yesterday's bill is safe: read it back, and add today's orders below it.
Remember: r = read, w = write fresh, a = add to the end.
Try it yourself: Run the append part twice, then read the file again. How many Adrak lines are there? Change "a" to "w" and run it. What happened to the old bill?
Code:
with open("bill.txt", "r") as f:
    bill = f.read()
print(bill)

with open("bill.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("\nAdrak: Rs 15")
Output:
Total: Rs 50

items.title: Python with Chai · Modules: the lucky chai
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 13: Modules: the lucky chai.
A module is a ready-made toolbox of code. You don't write it yourself, you import it.
random comes with Python. random.choice(list) picks one item from a list, a different one each run.
random.randint(1, 10) gives a whole number from 1 to 10, and both ends are included.
Remember: Don't build every tool yourself: import it.
Try it yourself: Add two more flavours to the list and run it 5 times. Did every flavour come up? Make a game: if the lucky number is 7, print "Chai free!"
Code:
import random

chai = ["Masala", "Adrak", "Elaichi"]
print("Aaj ki lucky chai:", random.choice(chai))

num = random.randint(1, 10)
print("Lucky number:", num)
Output:
Aaj ki lucky chai: Elaichi
Lucky number: 7
(run it again: you get new answers)

items.title: Python with Chai · f-strings: a neat bill
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 14: f-strings: a neat bill.
"Total: Rs " + total crashes with a TypeError : Python won't add text and a number.
An f-string has an f before the quotes. Anything inside { } is filled in with its value, no str() needed.
You can even do maths inside the braces: {total + 10} .
Remember: Put an f before the quotes, then fill in the { }.
Try it yourself: Add a variable flavour = "Masala" and print: Masala chai x 3 = Rs 50 Remove the f and run it again. What gets printed?
Code:
total = 50
cups = 3
print(f"{cups} cup chai: Rs {total}")
print(f"Tip ke saath: Rs {total + 10}")
Output:
3 cup chai: Rs 50
Tip ke saath: Rs 60

items.title: Python with Chai · range(): 10 cups at once
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 15: range(): 10 cups at once.
range(1, 11) is a counting machine: it gives 1, 2, 3 … 10. Put it in a for loop and 2 lines do the work of 10.
The stop number is never included: range(5) gives 0 to 4, and range(1, 6) gives 1 to 5.
A third number is the step : range(2, 11, 2) jumps by 2 and gives 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
Remember: range(start, stop, step): the stop never comes.
Try it yourself: Print the 5 times table: 5, 10, 15 … 50 (hint: a step of 5). Count down from 10 to 1 with range(10, 0, -1).
Code:
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(f"Cup {i} ready")

print(list(range(5)))
print(list(range(2, 11, 2)))
Output:
Cup 1 ready
Cup 2 ready
Cup 3 ready
Cup 4 ready
Cup 5 ready
Cup 6 ready
Cup 7 ready
Cup 8 ready
Cup 9 ready
Cup 10 ready
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

items.title: Python with Chai · Default values: less sugar
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 16: Default values: less sugar.
If a function needs a value and you don't give one, Python stops with a TypeError (missing argument).
A default value fixes that: def chai_banao(cheeni=1): uses 1 when you say nothing, and your value when you pass one.
Parameters with defaults go last : def chai_banao(size, cheeni=1) works, (cheeni=1, size) is a SyntaxError.
Remember: Default = the answer Python uses when you say nothing.
Try it yourself: Add a second parameter size="cutting" and print both values. Call chai_banao(cheeni=2). Does naming the argument work too?
Code:
def chai_banao(cheeni=1):
    print(f"Cheeni: {cheeni} chammach")

chai_banao()
chai_banao(0)
chai_banao(3)
Output:
Cheeni: 1 chammach
Cheeni: 0 chammach
Cheeni: 3 chammach

items.title: Python with Chai · Sets: how many customers?
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 17: Sets: how many customers?.
A list keeps duplicates: Ravi came twice, so len(log) says 4 when only 3 people came.
A set keeps each value only once: set(log) drops the double, and len() gives the real count.
add() puts in a new value (an existing one changes nothing), and in answers True or False. A set has no fixed order.
Remember: Set = a guest list with no doubles.
Try it yourself: Add "Ravi" again with add(). Did len(unique) change? Turn the set back into a list with list(unique) and print it.
Code:
log = ["Ravi", "Neha", "Ravi", "Amit"]
unique = set(log)
print(len(log), len(unique))

unique.add("Sita")
print("Ravi" in unique, "Zoya" in unique)
print(len(unique))
Output:
4 3
True False
4

items.title: Python with Chai · datetime: shop timing
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 18: datetime: shop timing.
datetime is Python's clock. from datetime import datetime brings it in, and datetime.now() gives the date and time right now.
strftime() formats it: "%H:%M" gives 09:30, "%d-%m-%Y" gives 18-10-2026.
now.hour is just the hour (0–23), so you can decide things: is the shop open?
Remember: datetime = Python's clock: now(), strftime(), hour.
Try it yourself: Print just the day name with now.strftime("%A"). Change the hours so the shop opens at 7 and closes at 11 at night.
Code:
from datetime import datetime

now = datetime.now()
print(now.strftime("%d-%m-%Y %H:%M"))

if 8 <= now.hour < 22:
    print("Dukaan khuli hai!")
else:
    print("Kal aana!")
Output:
18-10-2026 09:30
Dukaan khuli hai!
(your date and time will be different)

items.title: Python with Chai · Classes: the chai shop
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 19: Classes: the chai shop.
Two shops with separate variables ( dukaan1_naam , dukaan2_cups …) get messy fast. A class is the blueprint of one shop.
__init__ sets up each new shop, and self means "this shop": self.naam , self.cups .
A function inside the class is a method . Each object (raju, pappu) keeps its own count.
Remember: Class = the blueprint, object = a real shop.
Try it yourself: Add a third shop for "Sita" and sell 3 cups there. Add a method hisaab(self) that prints how many cups the shop has sold.
Code:
class ChaiDukaan:
    def __init__(self, naam):
        self.naam = naam
        self.cups = 0

    def bechna(self):
        self.cups += 1
        print(self.naam, self.cups)

raju = ChaiDukaan("Raju")
pappu = ChaiDukaan("Pappu")
raju.bechna()
raju.bechna()
pappu.bechna()
Output:
Raju 1
Raju 2
Pappu 1

items.title: Python with Chai · Finale: you know Python!
items.text:
Python with Chai, lesson 20: Finale: you know Python!.
Parts 1–10, the basics: variables, functions, if-else, lists, for loops, dictionaries, input, try-except and while True.
Parts 11–19, the pro moves: files (r, w, a), import random, f-strings, range(), default values, sets, datetime and classes.
Small ideas combine into real programs. Next stop: the AI + Python course , where the chai shop gets its own chatbot.
Remember: You know Python. Next: AI + Python, the chai chatbot.
Try it yourself: Turn this into a ChaiDukaan class with a method that serves 3 random cups. Save the cups to a file with "a" so every run adds to the bill.
Code:
import random

for i in range(1, 4):
    chai = random.choice(["Masala", "Adrak"])
    print(f"Cup {i}: {chai}")
Output:
Cup 1: Adrak
Cup 2: Masala
Cup 3: Masala
(random: your cups will be different)

items.title: AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot · Build a chai chatbot!
items.text:
AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot, lesson 1: Build a chai chatbot!.
A chatbot is a program that talks with you: you type, it replies.
You only need 3 things, all of which you learned in Python with Chai:
input() = listen · print() = reply · while True = keep going.
Our first Chai Bot is still simple: it says "Chai ready!" to everything. The next lessons make it smarter.
Remember: Chatbot = listen + reply + keep going.
Try it yourself: Change the bot's reply, for example to "Bot: Give me 2 minutes!". Make the bot say "Come again!" after "bye".
Code:
while True:
    msg = input("Aap: ")
    if msg == "bye": break
    print("Bot: Chai ready!")
Output:
Aap: menu
Bot: Chai ready!
Aap: kaise ho?
Bot: Chai ready!
Aap: bye

items.title: AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot · Teach the bot to reply (if-else)
items.text:
AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot, lesson 2: Teach the bot to reply (if-else).
In Part 1 the bot said "Chai ready!" to everything. Now it gets a brain: if-else .
if checks the first condition, elif (else if) checks the next one, and else catches everything else.
Python checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that matches.
Remember: if-else is the bot's brain.
Try it yourself: Add an elif for "hello" that replies "Namaste!". Type "MENU" in capitals. Why does the bot not understand? (Part 4 fixes this.)
Code:
while True:
    msg = input("Aap: ")
    if msg == "bye": break
    if msg == "menu": print("Masala, Adrak!")
    elif msg == "price": print("Rs 20")
    else: print("Samjha nahi!")
Output:
Aap: menu
Masala, Adrak!
Aap: price
Rs 20
Aap: kaise ho?
Samjha nahi!

items.title: AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot · 50 if-elses? Use a dictionary
items.text:
AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot, lesson 3: 50 if-elses? Use a dictionary.
Every new question meant another elif . With 50 questions the code gets long and messy.
A dictionary is the bot's answer diary: each question (the key ) points to its answer (the value ).
replies.get(msg, "Samjha nahi!") looks up the answer and falls back to the default when the question is missing.
Remember: A dictionary is the bot's diary: new question = one new line.
Try it yourself: Add "timing": "Subah 7 - raat 10" to the dictionary. How many lines did it take? Type "Menu" with a capital M. Why does it fail? (Part 4 fixes this.)
Code:
replies = {"menu": "Masala, Adrak!",
           "price": "Rs 20"}
while True:
    msg = input("Aap: ")
    if msg == "bye": break
    print(replies.get(msg, "Samjha nahi!"))
Output:
Aap: menu
Masala, Adrak!
Aap: price
Rs 20
Aap: kaise ho?
Samjha nahi!

items.title: AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot · "MENU" or "menu"? .lower() + .strip()
items.text:
AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot, lesson 4: "MENU" or "menu"? .lower() + .strip().
A customer types "MENU" with Caps Lock on, or adds a space by mistake: " menu". The Part 3 bot replies "Samjha nahi!", because its diary only has "menu".
For Python, "MENU", "menu" and " menu" are three different strings.
.lower() makes every letter small. .strip() removes extra spaces at the start and the end. Add both right after input() : clean the message first, then look it up.
• msg.lower() on its own line changes nothing. Strings never change, so keep the result: msg = msg.lower() .
• The dictionary keys must be lowercase too: "menu" , not "Menu" .
• .strip() only trims the ends. The space inside "masala chai" stays.
Remember: Clean it first, then look it up. (Pehle saaf karo, phir dhundo.)
Try it yourself: Press Run: the Input box already has " MENU ", "Price" and "menu".

items.title: AI + Python: Build a Chai Chatbot · "MENU" or "menu"? .lower() + .strip()
items.text:
Then try " menu " and "PRICE". Add "timing": "Subah 7 - raat 10" and type "TIMING". Remove .strip() and type " menu" with a space in front. What happens?
Code:
replies = {"menu": "Masala, Adrak!", "price": "Rs 20"}
while True:
    msg = input("Aap: ").lower().strip()
    print(replies.get(msg, "Samjha nahi!"))
Output:
Aap:   MENU 
Masala, Adrak!
Aap: Price
Rs 20
Aap: menu
Masala, Adrak!

items.title: Agentic AI with Bunty · Chatbot vs agent
items.text:
Agentic AI with Bunty, lesson 1: Chatbot vs agent.
Ask ChatGPT to "book my Goa trip" and it writes a long answer. No ticket or hotel actually gets booked.
A chatbot (Bunty version 1) only gives advice: "Sir, you could write the email like this…". You still do the work yourself.
An agent (Bunty version 2) has a laptop, email and a calendar. It finds a free slot, sends the email and tells you the meeting is fixed.
An agent has three extra things:
• Goal : you give it a task, not a question.
• Tools : email, browser, calendar, so it can act in the world.
• Loop : act, check the result, decide the next step, until the job is done.
Remember: A chatbot tells you; an agent does it.
Try it yourself: Write down 3 of your daily tasks. For each one, what would a chatbot do, and what would an agent do? Which tools would the agent need?

items.title: Privacy: What stays on your device
items.text:
What stays on your device
Lesson progress is saved in your own browser (local storage). It is never sent to us or anyone else. Clearing this site's data in your browser removes it.
Email updates (only if you sign up)
• If you enter your email in a “Get new lessons by email” box, we use it only to tell you when a new lesson or episode is published.
• You are added only after you click the confirmation link we email you.
• Your address is stored with our email service, Brevo, which sends the emails for us. We never sell or share it, and we never send ads.
• Our emails may record whether they were opened or a link was clicked, so we learn which lessons are useful.
• Every email has an unsubscribe link. To have your address deleted completely, write to samjhowithraj@gmail.com .

items.text:
Workshop enquiries and the cohort waitlist
If you send a workshop enquiry or join the Live Cohort waitlist, we use your details only to reply or to tell you when the cohort opens. They are kept with Brevo, like the email updates, and never sold or shared. Until those forms are connected, they open your own email app instead and nothing is stored here.
